triage.name: Transient tachypnea of the newborn
triage.reason: Term or near-term infant, often after cesarean delivery, with early tachypnea that resolves; a classic neonatal respiratory distress look-alike reachable by history, exam and chest x-ray.

demographics: Most common in late preterm and early term infants

risk_factors.text: Late preterm or early term birth

chief_complaints.text: My baby's nose is flaring and chest is pulling in

hpi.onset: Within the first 6 hours after birth, often immediately after delivery
hpi.duration: Usually resolves by 72 hours, but can last up to 5 days
hpi.progression: Tachypnea appears shortly after birth, is usually worst in the first 24 hours, then gradually improves. Significant worsening after initial stabilization should suggest another diagnosis.
hpi.location: Breathing difficulty without a focal painful area
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; occasionally needs supplemental oxygen or CPAP
hpi.timing: Continuous from birth, often more noticeable with crying or feeding

associated_symptoms.text: Sinking between or below the ribs

pertinent_negatives: Severe cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen

argues_against: Cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen

general.mild: Alert and active; tachypneic but no significant retractions; pink on room air
general.moderate: Tachypneic with nasal flaring and grunting; intercostal and subcostal retractions; may be irritable but consolable; oxygen saturation slightly low
general.severe: Marked respiratory distress with prominent retractions, grunting, nasal flaring; cyanotic on room air; may be lethargic or difficult to console
general.critical: Severe respiratory distress or impending respiratory failure; profound retractions, cyanosis despite oxygen, poor air entry, hypotonia, bradycardia or hypotension

findings.maneuver: Observe the infant's breathing rate and pattern while quiet
Observe the nares during quiet breathing
findings.finding: Widening of the nostrils with each breath

findings.maneuver: Listen for expiratory sounds without a stethoscope or with a stethoscope at the mouth
Inspect the chest wall between the ribs
findings.finding: Inward movement of the skin between the ribs during inspiration

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lower chest below the rib margin
findings.finding: Inward movement below the ribs during inspiration

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, tongue, and mucous membranes in good light
findings.finding: Bluish discoloration of lips or perioral area

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the chest in all fields
findings.finding: Fine crackles or rales on inspiration, often bilateral

findings.maneuver: Auscultate both sides of the chest symmetrically
findings.finding: No decreased or asymmetric breath sounds
No murmur; normal S1 and S2
Liver edge not more than 2 cm below the right costal margin

labs.caveat: Arterial blood gas is not routine; when obtained, hypoxemia is often mild and ventilation is usually adequate.

findings.text: Prominent pulmonary vascular markings, particularly in the perihilar regions
Fluid in the interlobar fissures, especially the right horizontal fissure

initial.why: Shows characteristic findings and helps exclude other causes of neonatal respiratory distress
Assesses severity of hypoxemia and ventilation
initial.only_if: significant respiratory distress, cyanosis, or oxygen requirement beyond low-flow
maternal risk factors for sepsis or infant appears ill
maternal risk factors for sepsis or infant appears ill

supporting.why: Adds to sepsis evaluation; normal in uncomplicated TTN

supporting.only_if: cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen, murmur, or cardiomegaly

not_indicated.why: No role in neonatal respiratory distress from TTN

decision_points: Chest x-ray, not CT or ultrasound, is the first imaging study in neonatal respiratory distress
Oxygen saturation monitoring is essential; arterial blood gas only for significant distress
Sepsis evaluation is not routine for every TTN infant but should be considered with maternal fever or instability
Do not obtain an ECG unless arrhythmia or congenital heart disease is suspected

differential.name: Neonatal sepsis / pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Presents in the first hours after birth with tachypnea, grunting, and retractions, just like TTN; early-onset sepsis must be excluded.
differential.trigger: Maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, or temperature instability in the infant

imaging: Chest x-ray may show patchy infiltrates or be normal
No classic TTN pattern of perihilar streaky densities and fissure fluid

differential.name: Respiratory distress syndrome
differential.why_considered: Severe respiratory distress from surfactant deficiency in a preterm or late preterm infant

history: Symptoms worsen over the first 24-48 hours rather than improve
labs: Blood gas shows worsening hypoxemia and respiratory acidosis
imaging: Diffuse reticulogranular ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms
Low lung volumes, unlike the hyperinflation sometimes seen in TTN

differential.name: Cyanotic congenital heart disease
differential.why_considered: Tachypnea and cyanosis in a term infant without significant retractions or lung disease
differential.trigger: Cyanosis that does not improve with supplemental oxygen or a murmur

history: Cyanosis from birth or first hours
exam: Weak femoral pulses if left-sided obstruction
labs: Hyperoxia test: PaO2 remains <150 mm Hg on 100% oxygen
Metabolic acidosis from poor perfusion in some lesions
imaging: Chest x-ray may show cardiomegaly or abnormal pulmonary vascularity

differential.name: Pneumothorax
differential.why_considered: Sudden onset or worsening respiratory distress in an infant, especially after positive pressure or meconium
differential.trigger: Asymmetric breath sounds or sudden deterioration

history: Risk factors: meconium aspiration, positive pressure ventilation
Sudden worsening or asymmetric chest movement
exam: Decreased breath sounds on the affected side
imaging: Pleural line with absent vascular markings on chest x-ray

differential.name: Meconium aspiration syndrome
differential.why_considered: Respiratory distress in an infant born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid

labs: Blood gas may show severe hypoxemia and mixed acidosis if PPHN develops

differential.name: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
differential.why_considered: Severe hypoxemia out of proportion to CXR findings, often triggered by TTN, sepsis, or meconium
differential.trigger: Labile hypoxemia or pre/postductal saturation gradient

history: Birth asphyxia, sepsis, meconium, or sometimes antecedent TTN
labs: Preductal and postductal PaO2 difference >20 mm Hg or pulse oximeter gradient
imaging: Chest x-ray may be clear or show underlying TTN/other disease
Echocardiogram shows elevated pulmonary pressures and right-to-left shunt

severity.mild: Respiratory rate 60-75/min, minimal retractions, no supplemental oxygen or low-flow <30% FiO2, infant active and feeding; symptoms usually resolve by 24-48 hours.
severity.moderate: Respiratory rate 70-90/min, visible retractions, grunting and nasal flaring, oxygen requirement 30-40% by nasal cannula, mild feeding difficulty; symptoms usually resolve by 48-72 hours.
severity.severe: Respiratory rate >90/min, marked retractions, cyanosis on room air, oxygen requirement >40% or need for CPAP; can last 3-5 days and require NICU care.
severity.critical: Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation; profound retractions, cyanosis despite oxygen, apnea, bradycardia or hypotension; progression to critical is rare but possible in severe TTN.

red_flags.meaning: Not typical for TTN; evaluate for RDS, sepsis, pneumothorax, or PPHN

red_flags.finding: Cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen
red_flags.meaning: Suspect cyanotic congenital heart disease or persistent pulmonary hypertension

red_flags.finding: Asymmetric breath sounds or sudden deterioration
Temperature instability, poor perfusion, or hypotension
red_flags.meaning: Early-onset neonatal sepsis must be ruled out

red_flags.finding: Need for more than 40% oxygen or mechanical ventilation
red_flags.meaning: Severe disease; reassess diagnosis and consult NICU

special_populations.differences: Late preterm and early term infants are most often affected; their course may be more prolonged and they more often need respiratory support.

key_questions.question: When did the fast breathing start?
key_questions.looking_for: Within the first 6 hours after birth, often immediately after delivery

key_questions.question: Was the baby born vaginally or by cesarean, and was there labor?
How many weeks was the baby at delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Late preterm or early term (about 35-38 weeks)

key_questions.question: Does the baby grunt, flare the nose, or pull in between the ribs?
key_questions.looking_for: Grunting, nasal flaring, intercostal or subcostal retractions

key_questions.question: What color are the baby's lips, tongue, and face?
key_questions.looking_for: Pink or mild perioral cyanosis; sustained central cyanosis suggests cyanotic heart disease

key_questions.question: Has the baby needed oxygen? How much, and has it improved?
key_questions.looking_for: Low oxygen requirement that improves within 24-72 hours; persistent high FiO2 suggests alternative

key_questions.question: Was there meconium in the amniotic fluid?
key_questions.looking_for: Clear fluid; meconium suggests meconium aspiration syndrome

key_questions.question: Was there any maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, or positive group B strep?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; presence raises concern for early-onset sepsis

key_questions.question: How is the baby feeding? Is the baby active and consolable?
key_questions.looking_for: Normal or mildly reduced feeding; significant lethargy or refusal suggests sepsis or severe distress

key_questions.question: Any coughing, wheezing, or pauses in breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; cough, wheeze, or apnea suggest pneumonia, airway issue, or worsening disease

reasoning_points: Term or late preterm infant, most often after cesarean delivery without labor
Onset of tachypnea within the first hours after birth
Mild-to-moderate respiratory distress with grunting, nasal flaring, and retractions
No significant cyanosis, or cyanosis that responds to oxygen
Chest x-ray shows perihilar streaky densities, fluid in fissures, and mild hyperinflation
No evidence of infection, congenital heart disease, or meconium aspiration

easy: Term infant born by elective cesarean section without labor
Tachypnea begins within minutes to hours after birth
Mild retractions and nasal flaring, oxygen saturation >92% on room air or low-flow oxygen
Chest x-ray shows perihilar streaky densities and fluid in the fissures
Respiratory distress resolves by 24-48 hours with no deterioration
medium: Late preterm infant (35-36 weeks) or infant of diabetic mother
Moderate distress with oxygen requirement 30-40% via nasal cannula
Grunting, intercostal retractions, and mild cyanosis
Needs CPAP briefly, or symptoms last up to 72 hours
Overlap with respiratory distress syndrome or early sepsis makes diagnosis less obvious
hard: Infant with severe hypoxia requiring >40% oxygen or mechanical ventilation
Cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen, raising cyanotic heart disease
Sepsis risk factors (maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes) with a septic-appearing infant
Symptoms persist beyond 5 days, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Chest x-ray findings are atypical or coexist with infiltrates or pneumothorax
